sections.label: Overview
sections.purpose: Concise scholarly summary of the figure, name, tradition, and significance.
sections.body:
**Ymir** (*ymir*) ​— Primordial ‌Giant, Chaos · ‌Scream / ​Roar — is ​the first ​living being of ​the Norse ​cosmos: the frost-giant ‌who quickened ​out of the ​dripping rime in ‌Ginnungagap, the ​ancestor of all ‌giants, and ​finally the raw ‌material of ​the world itself, ​slain by ​[[odinn|Óðinn]], Vili, and ​Vé and ​made into earth, ‌sea, mountains, ​and sky.[^1]

Old ‌Norse *Ymir* ​is most strongly ‌connected with ​the verb *ymja*, ‌'to scream, ​roar, resound' — ‌the Roarer ​— while a ​second line, ‌old and still ‌defended, derives the ‌name from ​Indo-European *yemo-*, 'twin', ​comparing Sanskrit ‌[[yama|Yama]]; both Simek ​and de ​Vries register the ‌dispute, and ​this edition does ​not pretend ‌it is settled.[^2] ​His mythology ‌is cosmogony entire: ​Völuspá opens ​its memory 'in ​early days, ​when Ymir dwelled', ‌Vafþrúðnismál gives ‌his birth from ​Élivágar's poisoned ‌rime and his ​self-begetting brood, Grímnismál ​catalogues the ‌world made from ‌his dismembered ‌body, and Hyndluljóð ‌states the ​doctrine that all ‌giants descend ​from him.[^3]

PuniCodex ​restores the ​name as **Ymir** ‌— identical ​to the ASCII ​input, because ​normalized Old Norse ‌writes no ​diacritic in this ​name — ​which the project's ‌mechanical rule ​places in Tier ‌2. The ​plain-ASCII domain **ymir.com** ‌is registered to ​a third ‌party outside the ‌PuniCodex collection ​and is watched ​for release; ​this temple claims ​no domain ‌and lives at ‌its canonical ​lexicon address.[^4]

sources.citation: Snorri Sturluson, Edda, Gylfaginning 5–8 (Ymir's origin, Auðhumla, the killing and the making of the world), ed. and trans. Anthony Faulkes (London: Everyman, 1987).

de Vries, Jan, Altnordisches etymologisches Wörterbuch, 2nd ed. (Leiden: Brill, 1962), s.v. Ymir; Simek, Rudolf, Dictionary of Northern Mythology, trans. Angela Hall (Cambridge: D. S. Brewer, 1993), s.v. Ymir.
Völuspá 3–5; Vafþrúðnismál 20–21, 29–35; Grímnismál 40–41; Hyndluljóð 33 (Poetic Edda), trans. Carolyne Larrington, The Poetic Edda, 2nd ed. (Oxford: Oxford University Press, 2014).

sections.label: The Name
sections.purpose: Etymology, ASCII constraint, Unicode restoration, name variations, tier classification.
sections.body:
The name ​is attested in ‌Old Norse as ‌**Ymir** (nominative; genitive ​*Ymis*). Its etymology ​is genuinely contested ​between two defensible ​lines, and honesty ​requires both. The ‌stronger philological line ​derives it from ​the Old Norse ‌verb *ymja*, 'to ​scream, roar, resound' ‌— the name ​would mean ‌'the Roarer, the ​Screamer', a fitting ​name for the ​bellowing primordial being ​the giants call ​Aurgelmir, 'mud-bellow'.[^1] The ‌alternative, favored in ​comparative scholarship, connects ‌*Ymir* with Indo-European ​*yemo-*, 'twin' — ‌Sanskrit [[yama|Yama]], Latin ​*geminus* — which ‌would suit the ​self-begetting, two-sexed primordial ‌from whose own ​body his children ​grew; de Vries, ‌Simek, and Lindow ‌all record the ‌dispute rather than ​resolve it.[^2] The ​given gloss 'Twin, ‌screamer (from *ymijaz)' ​follows the first ​line; the second ‌remains a live ​scholarly option.

The ​ASCII form is ‌not a ​compromise here: normalized ‌Old Norse *Ymir* ​is already written ​in plain ASCII ​letters. There is ​no diacritic, no ‌thorn or eth, ‌no vowel-length mark ​for the early ‌domain-name system to ​have stripped. The ​name is classified ‌Tier 2 by ‌the project's mechanical ‌rule — the ‌restoration preserves nothing ​the ASCII form ‌loses — which ​is a statement ​about orthography, never ​about the being ‌who fills the ​world's first chapter.

​The letter-by-letter transformation ​runs:

- **y** ‌→ **Y** — ​Same, capitalized
- ​**m** → **m** ​— Same
‌- **i** → ​**i** — Same
‌- **r** → ​**r** — Same

‌The project holds ​no domain for ‌this name: **ymir.com** ‌is registered to ​a third party ​outside the PuniCodex ​collection and is ​watched for release. ‌The temple lives ‌at its canonical ​lexicon address.

sources.citation: Cleasby, Richard, and Guðbrandur Vigfússon, An Icelandic-English Dictionary, 2nd ed. (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1957), s.v. Ymir, ymja; Zoëga, Geir T., A Concise Dictionary of Old Icelandic (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1910), s.v. Ymir, ymja.

Brewer, 1993), s.v. Ymir; Lindow, John, Norse Mythology: A Guide to the Gods, Heroes, Rituals, and Beliefs (Oxford: Oxford University Press, 2001), s.v. Ymir.

sections.label: Pronunciation
sections.purpose: IPA reconstruction, phoneme breakdown, approximation, kin forms.
sections.body:
The reconstructed ​pronunciation of ‌the name is ‌**/ˈy.mir/** — ​Old Norse Reconstruction.[^1]

​Phoneme by ​phoneme:

- **Y-** ​— Close ​front rounded [y], ‌the vowel ​of German *ü* ​or French ‌*u*: lips pursed ​as for ‌'oo' while the ​tongue positions ‌for 'ee'; stressed, ​as every ​Old Norse word ​is, on ​the first syllable
​- **-mir** ‌— Voiced ​bilabial nasal [m], ‌short close ​front [i] as ‌in 'bit', ​and the trilled ‌alveolar [r] ​of the nominative ‌ending, sounded ​fully

For the ​modern speaker, ‌the closest approximation ‌is: 'EE-meer' ‌spoken with rounded ​lips — ​form the mouth ‌for 'oo', ​say 'ee' inside ​it, then ‌a short 'i' ​and a ​lightly trilled final ‌r, as ​in modern Icelandic ‌*Ymir*.

Kindred ​and historical forms ​of the ​name:

- **Old ​Norse** — ‌Ymir; the þulur ‌also name ​him Aurgelmir ('mud-bellow'), ‌Brimir, and ​Bláinn[^2]
- **Old ​Norse (verb)** ‌— ymja, 'to ‌scream, roar, ‌resound', the root ‌of the ​leading etymology
- ‌**Sanskrit** — ​[[yama|Yama]], 'Twin', first ​mortal and ​king of the ‌dead, the ​comparandum of ​the alternative etymology[^3]
​- **Modern ‌Icelandic** — Ymir, ​the name's ​unbroken living form

​Ymir is ‌Tier 2 by ​the mechanical ‌rule: the normalized ​Old Norse ‌form is already ​plain ASCII, ‌so the restoration ‌loses nothing ​in transit. The ​god-sized being ​outruns his small ​name — ‌a statement about ‌spelling, never ​about scale.

sources.citation: Gordon, E. V., An Introduction to Old Norse, 2nd ed. rev. A. R. Taylor (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1957), phonology and grammar.
Snorri Sturluson, Edda, Skáldskaparmál, þulur of the giants, trans. Faulkes (1987).
de Vries, Jan, Altnordisches etymologisches Wörterbuch, 2nd ed. (Leiden: Brill, 1962), s.v. Ymir.

sections.label: Original Script & Provenance
sections.purpose: Original writing system, transliteration steps, uncertainty markers, font/display notes.
sections.body:
The name ​is preserved ‌in medieval Icelandic ‌manuscripts in ​the Latin ​alphabet as **Ymir** ​— Old ​Norse (North Germanic), ​attested 13th ‌c. CE ​in the Codex ​Regius of ‌the Poetic Edda ​(GKS 2365 ‌4to) and ​in the Prose ‌Edda codices, ​recording material centuries ​older.[^1] Before ​the Latin ​bookhand, Old Norse ​names were ‌carved in the ​Younger Futhark; ‌no runic attestation ​of this ‌name survives, ​so the manuscript ‌form is ​the primary witness, ‌and the ​reconstructed carving ​ᚢᛘᛁᛦ (úr for ‌y, maðr, ‌íss, and ýr ‌ᛦ for ​the nominative ​-r) is a ‌normalization, not ​an inscription.[^2]

The ​scholarly rendering ‌proceeds step ​by step:

- ​The name ‌is a simplex, ​not a ‌compound: *Ymir*, genitive ​*Ymis*, with ​the regular ​masculine nominative ending ​*-r*.
- ‌The leading etymology ‌connects it ​to the ‌verb *ymja*, 'to ​scream, roar, ​resound' — the ‌Roarer; the ‌alternative derives ‌it from Indo-European ‌*yemo-*, 'twin', ​with Sanskrit [[yama|Yama]] ‌as comparandum. ​The dispute ​is genuine and ​recorded in ‌the handbooks.[^3]
- ​Old Norse ​orthography writes the ​name with ‌four plain ​Latin letters; there ​is no ​diacritic for the ‌ASCII alphabet ​to have ‌lost.
- The ​Unicode restoration ‌Ymir is therefore ​identical to ‌the ASCII ‌input — an ​honest Tier ​2 by the ​mechanical rule, ​and a ‌statement about orthography, ‌never about ​the being.

sources.citation: Gordon, E. V., An Introduction to Old Norse, 2nd ed. rev. Taylor (Clarendon Press, 1957); The Poetic Edda, trans. Larrington (2014), introduction (manuscripts).
Barnes, Michael P., Runes: A Handbook (Boydell Press, 2012).
de Vries, Jan, Altnordisches etymologisches Wörterbuch, 2nd ed. (Brill, 1962), s.v. Ymir; Cleasby & Vigfússon, s.v. Ymir, ymja.

sections.label: Domains & Attributes
sections.purpose: Sphere of influence, titles, epithets, domain cards.
sections.body:
**Ymir** ​governs the ‌three headings ‌of his ​own existence: ​the primordial ​first-being, the ​frost out ​of which ‌he came, ​and the ​creation his ‌body became.[^1]

​### The ‌Primordial

Before ​earth, sea, ‌or sky ​there was ​Ymir — ​Völuspá's first ​named being, ​the datum ‌from which ​the whole ‌Norse account ​of time ‌unfolds. He ​is not ‌a character ​with adventures; ‌he is ​the world's ​first fact.

‌### Frost

‌He condenses ‌from the ​rime of ​Élivágar where ‌it met ​the sparks ​of Múspell ‌in Ginnungagap ​— frost ​made flesh, ‌the ice-world ​given a ‌body, and ​the ancestor ​of the ​frost-giants who ​keep his ‌nature.

### ‌Creation

Slain ​by [[odinn|Óðinn]], ‌Vili, and ​Vé, he ​becomes the ‌cosmos: flesh ‌earth, blood ‌sea, bones ‌mountains, hair ​trees, skull ‌sky, eyelashes ​the wall ​of Miðgarðr, ​brains the ‌driving clouds.[^2]

​### The ​Giants' Ancestor

​Hyndluljóð states ‌it flatly ​— all ​giants descend ​from Ymir. ‌His brood, ​begotten from ‌his own ​body, is ‌the older ​generation of ‌the world's ‌substance, the ​kin the ​gods both ​fight and ​marry: [[odinn|Óðinn]]'s ‌own grandmother ‌is the ​giantess [[bestla|Bestla]].[^1]

sources.citation: Snorri Sturluson, Edda, Gylfaginning 5–8, trans. Faulkes (1987); Hyndluljóð 33 (Poetic Edda), trans. Larrington (2014).
Grímnismál 40–41 (Poetic Edda), trans. Larrington (2014).

sections.label: Symbols
sections.body:
Ymir ​has no ‌cult regalia; ‌his 'symbols' ​are the ​fixed furniture ​of the ​cosmogony itself ​— the ‌places and ​beings the ​tradition cannot ‌tell his ​story without:[^1]

‌- **Ginnungagap** ​— The ‌yawning void ​between the ​ice of ​Niflheimr and ​the fire ​of Múspell, ‌the ​unmade space ‌in which ​the first ‌being quickened
​- **Élivágar** ‌— 'The ​ice-waves', the ‌rivers whose ​poisoned drops ​froze and ‌grew until ‌a jotunn ‌arose from ​them (Vafþrúðnismál ​31)
- ‌**Auðhumla** — ​The primeval ​cow whose ‌four rivers ​of milk ​fed Ymir, ‌and ​whose licking ‌of the ​salty rime-stones ​freed [[buri|Búri]], ​grandfather of ​the gods
‌- **The ‌dismembered body** ​— The ‌map of ​the world: ​flesh earth, ‌blood sea, ‌bones mountains, ‌skull sky ‌— anatomy ​as geography[^2]
‌- **The ​four sky-dwarfs** ​— Norðri, ​Suðri, Austri, ‌and ​Vestri, set ​by the ​gods to ‌bear up ​the skull-vault ​of heaven ​at its ‌four corners
​- **The ‌lúðr** — ​The vessel ‌(chest or ​boat, the ‌word is ‌debated) on ​which Bergelmir ​and his ​wife rode ​out the ‌blood-flood that ‌drowned the ​frost-giants[^3]

sources.citation: Snorri Sturluson, Edda, Gylfaginning 5–8, trans. Faulkes (1987).
Grímnismál 40–41 (Poetic Edda), trans. Larrington (2014).
Vafþrúðnismál 35 (Poetic Edda), trans. Larrington (2014); Lindow, John, Norse Mythology (Oxford University Press, 2001), s.v. Bergelmir.

sections.label: Mythology
sections.purpose: Core myths, primary narratives, and textual evidence.
sections.body:
Ymir's mythology is ​the Norse creation account entire: ‌he exists to be ‌first — first life, first ​giant, first death.[^1]

### Out ​of the Rime (Gylfaginning ​5–6; Vafþrúðnismál 20–21)

Before the ​world there was Ginnungagap, the ​yawning void, with the frozen ‌rivers of Niflheimr to ​the north and the sparks ​of Múspell to the south. ‌Where heat met rime, the ​hoar-frost melted and dripped, ‌and the drops quickened into ​the shape of a man: ‌Ymir, whom the frost-giants ​call Aurgelmir. Vafþrúðnismál gives the ​verse version — from Élivágar's ​waves shot poison-drops that froze ​and grew until a ​jotunn arose.[^1]

### The Self-Begetting ‌Giant (Vafþrúðnismál 29, 32–33)

Asked ​how Ymir got children when ‌he knew no giantess, ​Vafþrúðnir answers with the strangest ‌genealogy in the corpus: from ​under the giant's arm ‌grew a man and a ​woman together, and one leg ‌begot a six-headed son on ​the other. Hyndluljóð states ​the doctrine flatly — all ‌giants descend from Ymir.[^2]

### ‌Auðhumla and Búri (Gylfaginning 6)

‌From the same dripping ​rime came the cow Auðhumla; ​four rivers of milk fed ‌the giant, and she ​licked the salty rime-stones until ​[[buri|Búri]] emerged — hair the ‌first day, head the second, ​the whole man the ​third. Búri begot Borr, Borr ‌married the giantess [[bestla|Bestla]], and ​their sons were [[odinn|Óðinn]], Vili, ‌and Vé. Gods and ​giants rise from the same ​frost within days of one ​another.[^1]

### The Making ​of the World (Grímnismál 40–41; ‌Gylfaginning 8)

The three brothers ‌kill Ymir, and from his ​body they make the ‌world: from his flesh the ​earth, from his blood the ​sea, from his bones the ‌mountains, from his hair ‌the trees, from his skull ‌the sky; from his eyelashes ‌they built Miðgarðr as ​a defence against the giants, ‌and from his brains the ​heavy clouds. Snorri adds the ​maggots in the flesh, ​made rational as the dwarfs, ‌and the four dwarfs set ​to hold up the skull-vault. ​So much blood ran ​from the wound that the ‌frost-giants drowned in it — ​all but Bergelmir and ​his wife, who rode out ​the flood on their lúðr, ‌and from them the jotnar ​were born again.[^3]

### ‌'When Ymir Dwelled' (Völuspá 3–5)

​The völva of Völuspá opens ‌her memory with him: 'It ​was in early days, ‌when Ymir dwelled; there was ‌no sand nor sea nor ​cool waves.' The poem ​never stages the killing; it ​places Ymir on the far ​side of a before and ‌an after — the ‌name Norse tradition gives the ​raw, unworked world.[^4]

sources.citation: Snorri Sturluson, Edda, Gylfaginning 5–8, trans. Faulkes (1987); Vafþrúðnismál 20–21, trans. Larrington (2014).
Vafþrúðnismál 29, 32–33; Hyndluljóð 33 (Poetic Edda), trans. Larrington (2014).

sections.label: Syncretism & Reception
sections.purpose: Cross-cultural identification, later adaptations, and interpretatio.
sections.body:
Ymir stands ​at the ‌centre of ‌the best-known ​comparative debate ​in Germanic ​mythology: the ​Indo-European dismemberment ​cosmogony. The ‌Sanskrit parallel ​is exact ​in structure ‌— Rigveda ​10.90, the ‌Puruṣasūkta, makes ​the world ‌from the ​sacrifice of ​the primeval man ​Puruṣa, whose ​breath became ​wind, head ‌sky, feet ​earth — ‌and Bruce ​Lincoln's comparative ‌studies read ​Ymir as ‌the Norse ​reflex of ‌the same ​inherited creation ​pattern, complete ‌with the ‌'twin' and ‌'first sacrifice' motifs.[^1]

​The name ​itself is ‌the debate's ​second front. ​The 'twin' ‌etymology pairs ​*Ymir* with ​Sanskrit [[yama|Yama]] ‌— first ​mortal, son ‌of the ​sun, king ​of the ​dead, whose ​name means ‌'twin' — ‌and both ​figures anchor cosmogonies; ‌the 'roarer' ​etymology from ​*ymja* is ‌philologically safer ‌and semantically ‌apt for ‌the bellowing ​Aurgelmir.[^2] Tacitus ‌supplies the ​Germanic corroboration: ​Germania chapter ​2 records ‌that the ​peoples sing ​of Tuisto, ​'a god ‌born of the ​earth', and ​his son ​Mannus as ‌their ancestors ​— and ‌Tuisto's name ​is regularly ‌read as ​'twin, two-fold'. ‌The pattern ‌is consistent: ​a primordial, ​doubled being ​at the ​root of ‌the world, ‌divided to ​make it.[^3]

sources.citation: Lincoln, Bruce, Myth, Cosmos, and Society: Indo-European Themes of Creation and Destruction (Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1986); Rigveda 10.90 (Puruṣasūkta).
de Vries, Jan, Altnordisches etymologisches Wörterbuch, 2nd ed. (Leiden: Brill, 1962), s.v. Ymir; Simek, Rudolf, Dictionary of Northern Mythology, trans. Hall (1993), s.v. Ymir.
Tacitus, Germania 2, ed. and trans. J. B. Rives (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1999).

sections.label: Cultural Legacy
sections.purpose: Modern influence, literature, art, popular culture, and contemporary practice.
sections.body:
Ymir's ​afterlife runs ‌wherever Norse ‌myth is ​retold at ​scale, ​usually under ​his own ​name. Robert ‌E. Howard's ​'The ​Frost-Giant's Daughter' ‌(1934) made ​its icy ‌heroine the ​daughter of ‌Ymir ​and carried ​the name ​into heroic ​fantasy; Marvel ​Comics ‌has kept ​Ymir the ‌frost giant ​in print ‌since ​1962 as ‌an antagonist ​of [[thor|Thor]]; ‌and the ​name ​recurs across ‌fantasy games ‌wherever frost-giants ‌are wanted, ​from ​Dungeons & ‌Dragons onward.[^1]

​In scholarship ​the figure ‌anchors ​the comparative ​project: Lincoln's ‌account of ​Indo-European creation ‌ideology is ​built ​around the ​Ymir material, ​and every ‌handbook — ‌Simek, ​Orchard, Lindow ‌— treats ​the 'roarer' ​versus 'twin' ‌question ‌as the ‌standard entry ‌on the ​etymology.[^2] Modern ‌Heathenry ​reads him ​as the ​necessary first ‌matter of ​the ​cosmos: not ​a villain ‌erased from ​the world ​but ​the body ‌the world ​is still ‌made of ​— flesh ‌underfoot, ​weather overhead. ‌The name ‌itself never ​left the ​North: ​Icelandic *Ymir* ​remains a ‌living, if ‌rare, given ​name.

sources.citation: Howard, Robert E., 'The Frost-Giant's Daughter' (1934); Lindow, John, Norse Mythology (Oxford University Press, 2001), s.v. Ymir (modern reception).
Lincoln, Bruce, Myth, Cosmos, and Society (Harvard University Press, 1986); Simek, Rudolf, Dictionary of Northern Mythology, trans. Hall (1993), s.v. Ymir.

sections.label: Archaeology & Material Evidence
sections.purpose: Sites, inscriptions, artifacts, and physical attestations.
sections.body:
Ymir ​is an ‌entirely textual ‌being: no ​runestone invokes ​him, no ​votive deposit ​names him, ​and no ‌image in ​the Norse ​visual record ‌can be ​securely ‌identified with ​him — ‌a silence ​that fits ​a cosmogonic ​first-being rather ​than a ​cult figure.[^1] ‌The material ​record of ‌his mythology ​is ‌the manuscript ​record. Vafþrúðnismál ‌and Grímnismál ​survive in ‌the thirteenth-century ​Codex Regius ​of the ‌Poetic Edda ‌(GKS 2365 ‌4to); Völuspá ​is preserved ​both there ‌and ​in the ​fourteenth-century Hauksbók; ‌Snorri's creation ​account rests ​on the ‌Codex Regius ​of the ‌Prose Edda ​and its ​related codices.[^2]

​Skaldic practice ​keeps ‌the giant ‌in the ​working vocabulary ‌of the ​poets: the ​þulur catalogued ‌in Skáldskaparmál ‌list Aurgelmir, ‌Brimir, and ‌Bláinn among ​the giant-names, ‌and kennings ​for ​giants and ​for the ‌sky (Ymir's ​skull) presuppose ​the cosmogony's ​currency in ‌pre-Christian verse. ​The comparative ​witnesses are ​themselves textual: ‌Rigveda 10.90 ​in ‌the Sanskrit ​manuscript tradition ‌and Tacitus' ​Germania in ‌the Latin ‌one — ​the dismemberment ​pattern preserved ​in writing ​on three ‌edges of ‌the Indo-European ​world.[^3]

sources.citation: Lindow, John, Norse Mythology: A Guide to the Gods, Heroes, Rituals, and Beliefs (Oxford: Oxford University Press, 2001), s.v. Ymir.
The Poetic Edda, trans. Carolyne Larrington, 2nd ed. (Oxford: Oxford University Press, 2014), introduction (manuscripts: Codex Regius, Hauksbók).
Snorri Sturluson, Edda, Skáldskaparmál, þulur, trans. Faulkes (1987); Lincoln, Bruce, Myth, Cosmos, and Society (Harvard University Press, 1986).

sections.label: Poetic Edda
sections.body:
The Poetic ​Edda gives ‌Ymir four ‌distinct voices ​of testimony. ​Völuspá opens its ​vision with ​him — ​'it was ‌in early ​days, when Ymir ​dwelled; there ‌was no ​sand nor ‌sea nor ​cool waves' — ‌placing the ​giant as ​the poem's ​first named ​being and the ​marker of ‌the world's ​before.[^1] Vafþrúðnismál ‌is his fullest ​verse dossier: ‌[[odinn|Óðinn]], disguised ​as Gangráðr, ‌draws from ​the wise giant ‌Vafþrúðnir the ​whole genealogy ​— Ymir's ‌rise from ‌Élivágar's poisoned rime, ‌the man ​and woman ​grown under ‌his arm, ​the six-headed son ​begotten leg ‌on leg, ​and Bergelmir's ​survival of ‌the flood on ​his lúðr ‌'countless winters ​before the ​earth was ​made'.[^2]

Grímnismál supplies ​the creation ‌catalogue in ‌its purest ​form: 'From ‌Ymir's flesh the ​earth was ​shaped, and ‌from his ‌blood the ‌sea, mountains from ‌his bones, ​trees from ‌his hair, ​and from ​his skull the ​sky; and ‌from his ​eyelashes the ​cheerful gods made ​Miðgarðr for ‌men's sons; ​and from ​his brains ​the hard-minded clouds ‌were all ​created.'[^3] Hyndluljóð ‌closes the ​account with ‌the doctrine of ​descent — ‌all the ‌giants descend ​from Ymir ​— making him ​not merely ​the first ‌giant but ‌the race's ​common ancestor.[^4]

sources.citation: Völuspá 3–5 (Poetic Edda), trans. Larrington (2014).
Vafþrúðnismál 20–21, 29–35 (Poetic Edda), trans. Larrington (2014).
Grímnismál 40–41 (Poetic Edda), trans. Larrington (2014).
Hyndluljóð 33 (Poetic Edda), trans. Larrington (2014).

sections.label: Prose Edda
sections.body:
The ​Prose Edda ‌is Ymir's ‌narrative home. ​Gylfaginning 5–8 ​builds the ​cosmogony as ​continuous prose: ​Ginnungagap and ‌the ​eleven rivers ​of Élivágar ‌flowing with ​poison; the ‌meeting of ​Niflheimr's rime ‌and Múspell's ​sparks; the ​dripping ​that quickened ​into Ymir; ​the cow ‌Auðhumla and ​her four ‌rivers of ​milk; the ‌freeing ​of [[buri|Búri]] ‌from the ​licked rime-stones; ‌the marriage ​of Borr ​and [[bestla|Bestla]]; ‌and the ‌three brothers' ‌killing ​of the ​giant.[^1]

Snorri's ‌craft shows ​in the ​ordering of ‌the aftermath. ​The blood-flood ​that drowns ‌the ​frost-giants comes ‌first — ​catastrophe before ​construction — ​and only ​then the ‌making: earth ‌carried into ​the ‌middle of ​Ginnungagap, the ​sea ringed ‌around it, ‌the skull-vault ‌lifted by ‌the four ​dwarfs, the ‌sparks ​of Múspell ​fixed as ​stars, the ‌maggots in ​the flesh ​made rational ​as the ‌dwarfs, ​Miðgarðr walled ​with the ​eyelashes. Skáldskaparmál ‌then preserves ​the poetic ‌residue: the ​þulur name ‌the giant ​Aurgelmir, ‌Brimir, and ‌Bláinn, and ​the kennings ​for sky ​and giants ​keep the ‌cosmogony alive ‌as working ​imagery.[^2]

sources.citation: Snorri Sturluson, Edda, Gylfaginning 5–8, trans. Faulkes (1987).
Snorri Sturluson, Edda, Skáldskaparmál, þulur and kennings, trans. Faulkes (1987).

sections.label: Runic Evidence
sections.body:
The ​runic corpus ‌contains ‌no attestation ​of ​Ymir. No ​runestone ​names him, ​no ‌amulet carries ​him, ​and no ‌inscription ​yet found ‌preserves ​any of ‌his ​bynames — ​a ​silence he ​shares ​with the ‌whole ​cosmogonic stratum ‌of ​Norse myth ‌and ​one that ‌marks ​him as ‌a ​figure of ​poetry ‌and learned ‌prose ‌rather than ​of ​dedicatory practice.[^1]

‌What ​the runic ​tradition ‌does preserve ​is ​the alphabet ‌in ​which the ‌name ​would have ​been ​carved: the ​Younger ‌Futhark, in ‌use ​from the ‌eighth ​century, would ​write ‌*Ymir* as ‌ᚢᛘᛁᛦ ‌— the ‌úr-rune ​ᚢ doing ‌duty ​for y ​as ​it does ‌for ​u, then ​maðr ​ᛘ, íss ‌ᛁ, ​and the ​ýr-rune ​ᛦ writing ‌the ​final nominative ‌-r. ​The reconstructed ‌carving ​is a ‌normalization, ‌not an ​attestation; ​the name's ​real ​inscriptional life ‌is ‌in the ​manuscripts.[^2]

sources.citation: Lindow, John, Norse Mythology: A Guide to the Gods, Heroes, Rituals, and Beliefs (Oxford: Oxford University Press, 2001), s.v. Ymir.
Barnes, Michael P., Runes: A Handbook (Woodbridge: Boydell Press, 2012), on the Younger Futhark inventory.

sections.label: Sagas & Medieval Sources
sections.body:
Beyond ​the Eddas, ‌Ymir's medieval ‌afterlife is ​genealogical ​and poetic ​rather than ​narrative. ​Snorri opens ‌the Prose ​Edda's frame ​with ‌the cosmogony ​because the ‌whole ​system of ‌skaldic kennings ​depends on ​it ​— the ​sky is ​'Ymir's ‌skull', the ​earth 'Ymir's ‌flesh', and ​the ‌sea 'Ymir's ​blood' in ‌the ​poets' working ‌metaphors, so ​that every ​recited ‌verse re-performs ‌the dismemberment.[^1]

‌The ​learned tradition ​kept the ‌giant in ​its ​genealogies as ‌well: the ​Edda's ​euhemerizing prologue ‌and the ​þulur treat ‌Aurgelmir ​as the ​root-name of ​the ​jotnar, and ‌Saxo Grammaticus, ‌though he ​never ‌stages Ymir's ​death, begins ​his ‌Gesta Danorum ‌with a ‌Danish past ‌in ​which giants ‌are the ​oldest ​inhabitants of ​the North ‌— the ​same ​doctrine of ​the giants' ‌priority ​that Hyndluljóð ​states in ​verse.[^2] The ‌skaldic ​record, not ‌the saga ​narrative, ‌is where ​Ymir lives ‌on: a ‌cosmogony ​compressed into ​kennings, carried ​in ​every ship- ‌and sky-metaphor ‌the poets ​made.

sources.citation: Snorri Sturluson, Edda, Skáldskaparmál (kennings for sky, earth, sea), trans. Faulkes (1987).
Saxo Grammaticus, Gesta Danorum, Preface and Book 1, trans. Peter Fisher, ed. Hilda Ellis Davidson (Cambridge: D. S. Brewer, 1979).

sections.label: Meditation & Reflection
sections.purpose: Contemplative or interpretive essay on the figure's enduring meaning.
sections.body:
Every ​cosmogony answers ‌the question ‌of what ​the world ​is made ​from; the ​Norse ​answer is ‌a body. ​Before there ​was matter ‌there was ​already a ‌being — ​and ‌so creation, ​in this ​telling, is ​never innocent. ​The ground ​is flesh, ‌the ​sea is ‌blood, the ​mountains are ‌bones that ​once walked. ‌The myth ​refuses ‌the comfort ​of an ​empty beginning: ‌someone had ‌to die ‌for there ​to be ​anywhere ‌at all.[^1]

​Yet the ​Edda does ‌not linger ​on the ​killing's guilt; ‌it ​lingers on ‌the fitting. ​Flesh to ​earth, blood ​to sea, ​skull to ‌sky ‌— the ​world is ‌a translation, ​part for ​part, of ‌the first ‌body into ‌the ‌lasting one. ​To live ‌in Miðgarðr ​is to ​live inside ​Ymir: behind ‌a ​wall of ​his eyelashes, ​under a ‌vault of ​his skull, ​walking his ​flesh. ‌The old ​name for ‌that intimacy ​is one ‌the modern ​world is ‌relearning — ‌that ​the environment ​is not ​around us ​but is ‌what we ‌are made ​of.

sources.citation: Grímnismál 40–41 (Poetic Edda), trans. Larrington (2014); Snorri Sturluson, Edda, Gylfaginning 8, trans. Faulkes (1987).
